main: 1 RA VEN-MCS: Target-Mass-Calibrated Windowed-Asynchronous Federated Data Completion for Mobile Crowdsensing under Two-Stage Non-Random Selection **** and Anfeng Liu Abstract—Mobile crowdsensing completion learns from up- dates selected through sensing opportunities, observation, and delivery. Selection correction can reconstruct a deployment- target reference, yet that reference may remain infeasible for the clients and aggregation constraints of a finite window. RA VEN- MCS bridges this gap in two steps: it reconstructs reference mass over atomic sensing units, then calibrates executable client weights under weight caps and effective-support constraints. The calibration program coordinates reference fidelity with deployment-group composition and accumulated under-service. Our analysis establishes ideal pooled target-moment recovery under compatible support, sequential identification, and cluster regularity, and bounds reference-induced calibration perturba- tions at a fixed window state. In two City Scanner protocols with real opportunities and controlled delivery, full RA VEN achieves the lowest mean group mismatch among five methods. Relative to TwoStage-H ´ajek, the best group comparator, reductions are 25.8% and 23.3% by ratios of seed means. Observation is controlled in one protocol and measured in the other. Matched- support comparisons distinguish reference correction from fea- sible projection, supporting group-alignment gains within the evaluated support and constraints. Index Terms—Mobile crowdsensing, federated learning, data completion, windowed asynchronous learning, non-random selec- tion, selection bias, target-mass alignment. I. INTRODUCTION Mobile crowdsensing (MCS) uses distributed mobile sen- sors to observe urban and environmental fields for appli- cations including traffic and air-quality monitoring [1]. Un- even sampling leaves spatial and temporal gaps, motivating data completion for wider coverage and downstream sensing tasks [2], [3], [4]. Federated learning shares model updates while keeping the underlying sensing records distributed [5]. Existing work spans completion representations, distributed training, and target-aware aggregation. Transfer and multi- scale methods exploit related sensing tasks and non-aligned observations [4], [6]. Although asynchronous learning accom- modates irregular updates [7], participation correction adjusts unequal client contributions [8]. FedIPW corrects enrollment and participation with population-summary calibration [9], while FedPALS matches known target label mixtures with This work was supported in part by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (U24A20248). *** and Anfeng Liu are with the School of Electronic Information, Cen- tral South University, Changsha, 410083, China (E-mail: ****@csu.edu.cn, afengliu@mail.csu.edu.cn). convex aggregation and sample-ESS regularization [10]. These approaches address representation, update timing, and popu- lation composition. Participation-bias mitigation [8], [11], [12] and asyn- chronous aggregation [7] concern updates, whereas sensing selection also acts within client records. Population cali- bration [9] and target matching [10] do not automatically make corrected references executable under window-specific caps and effective-support constraints. Statistical reconstruc- tion therefore needs connecting to constrained execution and accumulated target service. To address the above challenges, we propose RA VEN-MCS (Reference Alignment Via Exposure-aware Normalization for Mobile CrowdSensing), a novel framework that reconstructs sensing-unit target references and calibrates executable client weights within finite windows. Specifically, opportunity (R), observation (O), and update usability (U) select records and updates sequentially. Lagged opportunity ratios and observa- tion propensities estimated without current responses supply correction weights for normalized local training and client ref- erence mass. Pre-outcome usability correction rescales client masses before reference normalization, retaining relative mass removed from local training. P2 calibrates this reference under weight caps and minimum effective support, coordinat- ing client-weight fidelity with deployment-group composition. Reweighting cannot create missing sensing support or ensure exact target matching. Debt records group under-service across windows; lagged variance and staleness proxies regularize de- cisions without inspecting current update vectors. Aggregation precedes debt and history updates, with debt computed from aggregate group composition. Design is configured before opening and fixed within each window, while coverage Gate remains diagnostic. Our theoretical analysis establishes ideal pooled target- moment recovery under correct ratios, compatible support, sequential identification, and cluster regularity, together with unique feasible calibration under convexity and a positive reference anchor, and reference-perturbation stability at a fixed window state. Experimental results show that full RA VEN achieves the lowest mean group mismatch among five methods in two City Scanner protocols with real opportunities and controlled delivery, with reductions of 25.8% and 23.3% relative to TwoStage-H ´ajek by ratios of seed means, using controlled and measured observation, respectively.

2 Our contributions follow. 1) We formulate deployment mass and sequential selection over atomic sensing units, with information boundaries connecting within-client correction to the between-client reference and supporting ideal pooled target-moment recovery. 2) We develop constrained window calibration linking ref- erence fidelity, group composition, and accumulated under-service, with fixed-state perturbation analysis sep- arating reference errors from limitations imposed by available support. 3) We evaluate group alignment and prediction under two City Scanner protocols, using matched-support compar- isons and separate geometry diagnostics to distinguish weighting mechanisms from limitations of available support. II. RELATEDWORK Sparse MCS studies evolutionary inference and sensing utility [2], [3], few-shot and cold-start transfer [6], [13], and uncertainty-based pricing [14]. Multi-scale methods use pyramids [15] or integrate non-aligned observations [4]; Struc- Former combines low-rank priors with Transformers [16], addressing representation rather than deployment mass. Federated completion [17] and FedAsync [7] address dis- tributed records and irregular updates. Staleness-aware meth- ods [18], [19], [20] improve timing and efficiency. DeFedAvg analyzes heterogeneous asynchronous training [21]; MasFL controls staleness through historical momentum, with adaptive gradient normalization in AdaMasFL [22]. FL bias includes demographic, performance-related, and contribution-related effects [23]; arbitrary participation has dedicated analyses [24]. FedAU estimates participation weights [8]; other methods handle correlated participation, semi-asynchronous bias, and opt-out stragglers [11], [12], [25]. FAST permits arbitrary participation between snapshots but requires uniform client participation at snapshots [26]. FOCUS uses time-varying graphs and push–pull updates, with linear rates under strong convexity or a Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition and positive participation probabilities [27]. PHP- FL targets performance fairness with unequal participation and heterogeneous models [28]. Selection also affects information within client records. Cafe personalizes imputation using missingness complementarity and observed sample size [29]; DARN uses these signals for direct incomplete-tabular prediction without imputation [30]. FedIPW [9] factors enrollment and participation, with population-summary calibration under limited information. FedPALS [10] uses convex target-label matching and an in- verse sample-ESS penalty, including targets beyond the client convex hull. RA VEN links atomic R/O/U reference reconstruc- tion to feasible window mixtures with hard client caps, client- level ESS, and target debt. IPW and H ´ajek estimation provide the tools [31], [32], [33], [34]; weighting need not improve neural-network prediction [35]. III.
